strengths: SFTMix addresses a relevant NLP problem with a simple recipe: interpolate final hidden states and token targets across confidence groups, and add the resulting Mixup objective to standard instruction tuning. It requires no additional response annotation, and the main pipeline is clearly explained.

The empirical coverage is substantial. Table 1 reports improvements across all seven tested model–dataset combinations, spanning three model families and datasets of different sizes and qualities. MT-Bench improvements are approximately 0.20–0.40 points, and AlpacaEval-2 length-controlled win-rate improvements are 0.32–1.67 percentage points.

Additional evidence supports the reported direction of improvement. Medical QA averages increase by 1.33 and 1.66 percentage points for Llama and Mistral, respectively. The human evaluation collects 200 judgments over 80 prompts and favors SFTMix over NTP, with 42.5% wins versus 26.5% losses and 31% ties.

The LoRA, data-selection, smaller-reference-model, and multilingual experiments provide useful preliminary evidence of applicability. Reusing the same hyperparameters across several settings also strengthens the evidence beyond the configuration used for tuning.
weaknesses: The central claim that confidence-based pairing is crucial lacks the decisive controlled comparison. There is no ordinary random-pair Mixup baseline, shuffled-confidence control, or comparison with confidence from a single checkpoint. Section 5.2 changes the response dataset and tests quality-based pairing, which does not isolate the benefit of confidence-based pairing on identical data. This omission also limits differentiation from existing cartography-based Mixup methods.

Appendix A.1 selects both hyperparameters using MT-Bench and AlpacaEval-2, the same benchmarks used for the reported results; no separate validation protocol is described. This creates selection bias, particularly for Llama/Alpaca and the many analyses using that configuration. Improvements on other configurations are reassuring, but an untouched evaluation and comparable baseline tuning are needed.

The reliability of the effect sizes is insufficiently characterized. No confidence intervals, significance tests, or clearly identified independent training-seed repetitions are reported. Averaging five evaluation rounds does not establish robustness to training randomness. The human evaluation likewise lacks uncertainty estimates accounting for repeated judgments on the same prompts, so claims of significant improvement are stronger than the reported evidence.

The mechanistic claims exceed the analysis. Separation in a t-SNE plot of extreme-confidence examples and a 7% reduction in training-confidence standard deviation do not demonstrate reduced overfitting on confident examples or improved generalization on unconfident ones. Section 3.4 establishes a generic property of Mixup gradients, without establishing those benefits. Section 5.3 is principally a loss-weight ablation, rather than evidence for a categorical distinction between a loss and a regularizer.

Reproducibility needs stronger documentation. The manuscript provides several optimization settings but omits the confidence-checkpoint schedule, prompt and truncation settings, LoRA configuration, exact GPT-4 judge version, and generation protocol. No implementation link is supplied. The human evaluation also leaves annotator counts, assignment, presentation randomization, and agreement unspecified. Together with the missing controls and validation separation, these gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation despite the encouraging empirical breadth.

The practical cost–benefit case remains incomplete. Default SFTMix requires reference-model fine-tuning and checkpoint scoring, but total GPU time, memory, and throughput are not quantified. The smaller-reference experiment is useful, yet there is no comparison against NTP under the same total compute budget or a relevant inexpensive regularizer such as NEFTune. This limits the broader efficiency and scalability claims.
